title: Customer Research and Effective Interview Questions
intro: Understanding your customers is crucial for developing products and services they truly need. This lesson will guide you through the principles of effective customer research, focusing on how to design and conduct interviews that reveal genuine insights into customer behavior and motivations. We'll explore the art of asking open-ended, neutral questions that uncover past experiences and actual actions, rather than relying on future promises or biased opinions. By mastering these techniques, you'll be able to gather reliable data that informs better business decisions and helps you avoid common pitfalls in customer feedback collection.
goals: Formulate open-ended interview questions that elicit detailed, unbiased customer responses
Distinguish between leading and neutral questions, and convert leading questions into effective neutral ones
Identify and avoid common biases in customer interviews, such as relying on future promises or small sample sizes
Develop a structured interview guide to systematically gather insights into customer experiences and behaviors

sections.title: The Core Concept of Customer Research
sections.text: Effective customer research goes beyond simply asking what people want. It's about understanding their actual behavior, past experiences, and the real problems they face. The most valuable insights come from observing or asking about recent, specific actions rather than hypothetical future scenarios. For instance, instead of asking if someone would use a faster service, inquire about the last time they encountered a delay and how they dealt with it. This approach helps uncover underlying needs and pain points that customers might not articulate directly if asked about future preferences. By focusing on the 'what' and 'how' of past actions, you gain a clearer picture of their current reality and the alternatives they currently use.
sections.reflection: Think about a recent purchase you made. What questions would a researcher ask you about that experience to understand your actual needs, rather than just your satisfaction with the product?

sections.title: Crafting Effective Interview Questions
sections.text: The quality of your customer insights directly depends on the quality of your questions. Effective interview questions are open-ended, neutral, and focus on past or present behavior. An open-ended question encourages a detailed response, moving beyond a simple 'yes' or 'no'. A neutral question avoids suggesting an answer, allowing the interviewee to share their genuine perspective without feeling led. For example, instead of asking, “Don't you agree our new app is user-friendly?”, ask, “Can you describe your experience using the new app?” Follow-up questions are also critical; they help clarify reasons or sequences of events, such as “Why did you choose that option?” or “What happened next?” This iterative questioning helps to dig deeper into the customer's thought process and actions.
sections.reflection: Consider a product or service you use regularly. How would you rephrase a leading question about it (e.g., 'Do you love how easy this is?') into a neutral, open-ended question?

sections.title: Applying Research to Real-World Scenarios
sections.text: Applying customer research principles means systematically gathering and interpreting data to inform product development or service improvements. When conducting interviews, always seek consent for recording, ensuring transparency and trust. During the interview, focus on active listening and avoid interrupting. After collecting responses, it's crucial to separate direct quotes from your interpretations. For example, if a customer says, “I often forget my password,” that's a quote. Your interpretation might be, “The customer experiences friction due to password recall issues.” This distinction helps maintain objectivity. The goal is to build a rich understanding of customer journeys, pain points, and motivations, which can then be used to identify opportunities for innovation or improvement that genuinely address user needs.
sections.reflection: Imagine you're interviewing a customer about their experience with online shopping. What are three specific things you would listen for to understand their actual behavior and not just their stated preferences?

sections.title: Limitations and Ethical Considerations
sections.text: While customer research is invaluable, it has limitations and ethical considerations. A key limitation is the sample size; insights from a small number of interviews cannot be generalized to the entire market. It's crucial to avoid making broad market conclusions based on limited data. Ethically, always minimize the data you collect, only gathering information directly relevant to your research goals. Protect interviewee privacy and ensure their responses are anonymized if not explicitly consented otherwise. Be mindful of confirmation bias, where you might unconsciously seek out information that confirms your existing beliefs. Strive for neutrality in your questioning and analysis to ensure the insights gained are as objective and representative as possible.
sections.reflection: Why is it problematic to conclude that 'all customers want X' after interviewing only five people who expressed a desire for X? What are the ethical implications of collecting too much personal data?

sections.title: Common Errors in Customer Interviews
sections.text: One of the most common errors in customer interviews is asking leading questions. These questions subtly guide the interviewee towards a desired answer, contaminating the data. For instance, asking, “Wouldn't you prefer a faster delivery option?” already implies that faster is better and that the current option is slow. Another error is relying on future promises or hypothetical scenarios. Customers might express enthusiasm for an untried idea, but this 'polite enthusiasm' rarely translates into actual purchase behavior. People often say what they think you want to hear or what they believe they *would* do, which can be very different from what they *actually* do. Always anchor questions in past actions or current realities to avoid these pitfalls.
sections.reflection: Recall a time someone asked you a leading question. How did it make you feel, and did it influence your answer? How could that question have been rephrased to be neutral?

sections.title: Transferring Insights into Action
sections.text: The ultimate goal of customer research is to transfer the insights gained into actionable steps for your business. This involves synthesizing the qualitative data from interviews to identify patterns, recurring pain points, and unmet needs. For example, if multiple customers describe struggling with a specific step in a process, that's a clear signal for improvement. The insights should directly inform product features, service design, or marketing messages. It's not enough to just collect data; you must analyze it critically, identify the root causes of customer behaviors, and translate these findings into concrete recommendations. This iterative process of research, analysis, and action ensures that your offerings are truly customer-centric and solve real problems.
sections.reflection: After conducting a series of customer interviews, what is the most important first step you would take to turn your findings into a practical improvement for a product or service?

example.title: Improving a Local Printing Service
example.text: This is a fictional learning case. A local printing shop wants to understand why some customers use their service for urgent jobs while others go elsewhere. They initially thought customers simply wanted faster machines. To investigate, they decided to conduct customer interviews, focusing on past experiences rather than asking about future desires for speed.
example.decision: The printing shop needs to design interview questions that uncover actual customer behavior and pain points related to urgent printing, avoiding leading questions about speed.
steps: **Step 1: Identify the core problem to investigate.** The initial assumption was 'customers want faster machines'. This might describe a surface-level symptom rather than the underlying problem. The real problem could be related to file preparation, proofing, or communication. The goal is to understand the entire customer journey for urgent printing needs.

**Step 2: Brainstorm leading questions and rephrase them neutrally.** An initial leading question might be: “Wouldn’t you love our super-fast printing service?” This implies speed is the main issue and suggests a desired answer. A neutral rephrasing would be: “Tell me about the last time you needed printing before a tight deadline.” This opens up the conversation to other potential issues.

**Step 3: Develop open-ended questions focusing on recent experiences.** Instead of asking hypothetical questions, focus on specific past events. Questions like: “Can you describe the steps you took from deciding you needed printing to picking up the final product?” or “What challenges did you face during that process?” will provide concrete details about their experience.

**Step 4: Include questions about alternatives and reasons.** To understand why customers might choose other services, ask: “What alternatives did you consider for that urgent printing job, and why did you choose us (or them)?” This helps uncover competitive advantages or disadvantages beyond just speed, such as cost, location, or specific material availability.

**Step 5: Plan for follow-up questions to clarify details.** Prepare to ask 'why' and 'how' questions to delve deeper into responses. If a customer mentions a delay, ask: “What caused that delay?” or “How did that impact your deadline?” This ensures a thorough understanding of the sequence of events and the customer's emotional response, revealing true pain points.

quiz.question: Which type of question is most effective for uncovering genuine customer needs?
options: Questions about future desires and preferences
Questions that confirm your product's benefits
Questions about recent actual experiences and behaviors
Questions that offer clear 'yes' or 'no' answers
quiz.explanation: Questions about recent actual experiences and behaviors provide concrete evidence of how customers interact with products or services, revealing real needs and pain points. Future desires are often unreliable, confirming questions are biased, and 'yes/no' questions lack depth.

quiz.question: A product team is developing a new coffee maker. Which of these questions is a leading question?
options: How often do you brew coffee at home?
What features are most important to you in a coffee maker?
Don't you agree that our new coffee maker's design is sleek and modern?
Describe your morning routine when making coffee.
quiz.explanation: 'Don't you agree that our new coffee maker's design is sleek and modern?' is a leading question because it suggests the desired answer (that the design is sleek and modern) and pressures the interviewee to agree. The other options are neutral and open-ended.

quiz.question: You are interviewing a customer about their online shopping experience. They say, 'I love how easy it is to find what I need.' What is the best follow-up question?
options: So, you think our website is very user-friendly?
Can you tell me about a specific time you found something easily?
Would you recommend our website to your friends?
What other websites do you find easy to use?
quiz.explanation: Asking 'Can you tell me about a specific time you found something easily?' is the best follow-up. It prompts the customer to provide a concrete example of their positive experience, moving beyond a general statement and providing actionable insights. The other options are either leading, ask for a future promise, or divert from the current experience.

quiz.question: What is a key ethical consideration when conducting customer interviews?
options: Collecting as much personal data as possible for future use
Generalizing findings from a small sample to the entire market
Obtaining consent for recording and minimizing collected data
Ensuring all interviewees praise your product or service
quiz.explanation: Obtaining consent for recording and minimizing collected data are crucial ethical considerations. It respects privacy and ensures data is used responsibly. Collecting excessive data, generalizing small samples, or seeking only praise are unethical or lead to biased results.

quiz.question: A startup is designing a new app. During interviews, several potential users express great enthusiasm for the app's concept, saying they 'would definitely use it.' What should the startup conclude from this?
options: The app is guaranteed to be a market success.
Future enthusiasm is a strong indicator of actual purchase behavior.
Polite enthusiasm for an untried idea does not guarantee actual usage.
The app should be launched immediately without further testing.
quiz.explanation: Polite enthusiasm for an untried idea does not guarantee actual usage. Customers often express positive opinions to be polite or because they genuinely like the idea, but this doesn't always translate into real-world adoption or purchase. Actual behavior is a stronger predictor than future promises.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes the purpose of separating direct quotes from your interpretations in customer research?
options: To make the research report longer and more detailed.
To avoid confusing the customer during the interview.
To maintain objectivity and ensure insights are based on actual customer statements.
To highlight your own opinions and biases in the analysis.
quiz.explanation: Separating direct quotes from interpretations helps maintain objectivity and ensures that the insights and conclusions drawn are directly supported by what the customer actually said, rather than being influenced by the researcher's biases or assumptions. It prevents misrepresenting customer feedback.

assignment.prompt: Design an interview guide for a fictional business. Your guide should include six open-ended questions designed to uncover customer behavior and needs, and then you will rewrite three leading questions into neutral, open-ended ones. Finally, simulate an interview by providing fictional responses and separating quotes from your interpretations.
criteria: Business description is clear and relevant to the interview questions.
Six open-ended questions effectively target customer behavior and needs.
Three leading questions are clearly identified and accurately rewritten as neutral.
Simulated responses are realistic and clearly distinguish between quotes and interpretations.
The overall interview guide demonstrates an understanding of effective questioning techniques.

rubric.excellent: Provides a clear, concise, and compelling description of a fictional business, setting appropriate context for the interview questions.
rubric.adequate: Provides a basic description of a fictional business, which generally sets the context for the questions.
rubric.needsRevision: Business description is vague, incomplete, or does not adequately set the context for the interview questions.

rubric.excellent: All six questions are genuinely open-ended, neutral, and expertly designed to elicit detailed insights into past customer behavior and specific experiences.
rubric.adequate: Most questions are open-ended and neutral, aiming to understand customer behavior, though some may lack depth or specificity.
rubric.needsRevision: Questions are predominantly closed-ended, leading, or fail to focus on past behavior and specific experiences.

rubric.excellent: Clearly identifies three distinct leading questions that demonstrate a strong understanding of what makes a question biased.
rubric.adequate: Identifies three questions that are somewhat leading, though the bias might not be overtly strong in all cases.
rubric.needsRevision: Fails to identify truly leading questions, or the questions provided are not clearly biased.

rubric.excellent: Successfully transforms all three leading questions into perfectly neutral, open-ended questions that effectively remove bias and encourage detailed responses.
rubric.adequate: Rewrites the leading questions into more neutral forms, though some may still retain a slight bias or could be more open-ended.
rubric.needsRevision: Rewritten questions remain leading, are not open-ended, or do not effectively remove the original bias.

rubric.excellent: Provides realistic and detailed fictional responses, with a clear and accurate separation of direct quotes from insightful interpretations, demonstrating strong analytical skills.
rubric.adequate: Offers plausible fictional responses and attempts to separate quotes from interpretations, though the distinction might sometimes be unclear or interpretations lack depth.
rubric.needsRevision: Fictional responses are unrealistic, lack detail, or fail to clearly separate direct quotes from personal interpretations.

faq.question: Why is it important to ask about past behavior instead of future intentions?
faq.answer: Past behavior is a much stronger predictor of future actions than stated intentions. People often express enthusiasm for new ideas or say what they think you want to hear, but their actual behavior in a real-world context provides concrete evidence of their needs, habits, and pain points. Focusing on 'what did you do?' rather than 'what would you do?' yields more reliable data.

faq.question: What is a 'leading question' and why should I avoid it?
faq.answer: A leading question is one that subtly prompts or encourages the interviewee to give a particular answer, often by including the desired answer within the question itself. For example, 'Don't you think our service is fast?' You should avoid them because they introduce bias, making the collected data unreliable as it reflects your assumptions rather than the customer's genuine perspective.

faq.question: How many interviews are enough to draw conclusions?
faq.answer: The number of interviews depends on your research goals. For qualitative insights into user experience and identifying common pain points, a small sample (e.g., 5-10 interviews) can reveal significant patterns. However, it's crucial to remember that these findings are qualitative and cannot be generalized statistically to an entire market. For broader market conclusions, quantitative research with a much larger, representative sample is needed.

summary: Effective customer research focuses on understanding actual past behaviors and experiences, not hypothetical future promises.
Crafting open-ended, neutral questions is crucial for eliciting unbiased, detailed responses from interviewees.
Always obtain consent for recording and minimize the data collected to ensure ethical research practices.
Avoid common errors like leading questions and generalizing insights from small sample sizes to the entire market.

title: Value proposition and business model
intro: In the competitive world of business, simply having a product or service isn't enough. You need to clearly articulate what unique value you offer and how your business operates to deliver that value sustainably. This lesson will guide you through defining your value proposition and mapping it to a coherent business model, ensuring your idea has a solid foundation for success.
goals: Define what a value proposition is and identify its key components.
Explain how a value proposition connects to the core elements of a business model.
Analyze a business model for coherence and identify potential inconsistencies.
Develop a basic value proposition and outline its corresponding business model elements.

sections.title: Understanding the Value Proposition
sections.text: A value proposition is a clear statement that explains what benefits a company provides, to whom, and why it's better than alternatives. It's not just about what you sell, but the problem you solve and the unique outcome you deliver for your customer. To construct a strong value proposition, you must identify your target customer, understand their specific problem or need, articulate the useful outcome or solution you offer, and explain why a customer should choose your offering over competitors or existing alternatives. This statement forms the core of your business idea, guiding all subsequent decisions. Without a clear value proposition, a business risks offering something nobody truly needs or failing to differentiate itself in the market.
sections.reflection: Think about a product or service you use regularly. What specific problem does it solve for you, and why do you choose it over other options?

sections.title: Connecting Value to the Business Model Canvas
sections.text: Once you have a clear value proposition, the next step is to connect it to a comprehensive business model. A business model describes how an organization creates, delivers, and captures value. Key components include customer segments (who you serve), channels (how you reach them), key activities (what you do), key resources (what you need), key partners (who helps you), revenue streams (how you make money), and cost structure (what expenses you incur). The value proposition sits at the heart of this model, influencing every other element. For instance, if your value proposition promises 'fast delivery,' your key activities must include efficient logistics, your resources might include a fleet of vehicles, and your cost structure will reflect these operational expenses.
sections.reflection: How might a value proposition focused on 'luxury experience' lead to different business model elements compared to one focused on 'affordability'?

sections.title: Practical Application: Building Your Model
sections.text: Applying the value proposition and business model concepts involves a structured approach. Start by clearly articulating your value proposition in one or two concise sentences. Then, systematically map this proposition to the various components of your business model. For each connection, consider the underlying assumptions. For example, if your value proposition is 'affordable, high-quality handmade jewelry,' an assumption might be that customers value handmade quality at a lower price point. You then need to devise a test for this assumption, such as conducting market surveys or running a small pilot sale. This iterative process of defining, connecting, assuming, and testing helps validate your business idea and refine your strategy before significant investment.
sections.reflection: Imagine you want to start a local coffee shop. What would be your two-sentence value proposition, and what is one key assumption behind it?

sections.title: Limitations and Challenges
sections.text: While powerful, the value proposition and business model framework have limitations. They are snapshots in time and require continuous re-evaluation as markets, customer needs, and technologies evolve. A common challenge is maintaining coherence across all elements. For example, promising 'premium, personalized service' while relying on automated, low-cost channels creates an inconsistency that will frustrate customers and undermine your value. Another limitation is the temptation to fill out the model's boxes without deep thought about the interdependencies. Simply listing resources or activities without linking them directly to value creation or cost implications can lead to a superficial and ultimately unworkable model. True value comes from the logical flow and alignment between all components.
sections.reflection: Can you think of a company that failed because its business model elements didn't align with its stated value proposition?

sections.title: Common Error: Resource vs. Value
sections.text: A frequent mistake is confusing a resource with a value proposition. Owning a state-of-the-art machine, having a prime location, or employing skilled staff are all valuable resources. However, they are not, by themselves, a value proposition. A value proposition must articulate the *benefit* these resources provide to the customer. For example, 'We own the fastest printing press' is a resource statement. A value proposition would be 'We help students avoid late submission penalties by providing guaranteed same-day, error-free document printing.' The printing press is a key resource enabling the value, but the value itself is the problem solved (late penalties) and the useful outcome (guaranteed, error-free printing). Always focus on the customer's gain, not just your assets.
sections.reflection: How would you rephrase 'We have experienced chefs' into a customer-centric value proposition for a restaurant?

sections.title: Transferring Concepts to New Contexts
sections.text: The principles of value proposition and business model design are highly transferable beyond traditional product-based businesses. They can be applied to service industries, non-profit organizations, internal corporate projects, and even personal career planning. For a non-profit, the 'customer' might be a beneficiary group, and the 'revenue' could be donations or grants, with the value proposition focusing on social impact. In career planning, you are the 'product,' your skills are 'resources,' and your 'value proposition' is what unique benefits you offer to a potential employer. The core idea remains: clearly define who you serve, what problem you solve, the unique outcome you provide, and how you deliver it sustainably.
sections.reflection: How could you apply the concept of a value proposition to your own personal skills and career aspirations?

example.title: Pre-Print File Checking Service for Students
example.text: This is a fictional learning case. A new service aims to help university students avoid common printing errors and delays. Students often submit files for printing only to find formatting issues, incorrect page sizes, or missing fonts, leading to wasted time, money, and missed deadlines. This service proposes to receive student files in advance, perform a thorough check for common issues, and confirm their print-readiness before the actual printing process begins.
example.decision: To develop a coherent business model that delivers on the value proposition of reducing rework and waiting for student printing, while ensuring operational feasibility and profitability.
steps: **Step 1: Formulate the Value Proposition.** The service helps university students save time and avoid stress by proactively checking their print files for errors, ensuring a perfect print on the first attempt and eliminating costly reworks and delays.

**Step 2: Connect Value Proposition to Business Model Elements.** Identify the core elements: Customer Segment (University Students), Channels (Online submission portal, campus kiosks), Key Activities (File checking, communication, printing), Key Resources (Specialized software, trained staff, printing equipment), Revenue Streams (Per-page fee, subscription options), Cost Structure (Software licenses, staff salaries, equipment maintenance).

**Step 3: Add Assumptions and Tests for Key Relationships.** For 'Online submission portal' (Channel), assume students prefer digital submission; test by surveying students. For 'Specialized software' (Resource), assume it can automate most checks; test by piloting with a sample of diverse student files. For 'Per-page fee' (Revenue), assume students will pay a small premium for error-free prints; test by offering a trial period.

**Step 4: Identify an Inconsistency.** Upon review, the value proposition promises 'proactively checking files' and 'eliminating costly reworks.' However, if the 'file checking' is primarily manual and time-consuming, it might contradict the 'eliminating delays' part of the value proposition, especially during peak periods. Manual checking could introduce new delays.

**Step 5: Repair the Inconsistency.** To resolve the conflict between manual checking and speed, the business model needs adjustment. The 'Key Resources' should explicitly include 'automated file analysis software' to handle common checks quickly. 'Key Activities' would then shift to 'automated initial checks' followed by 'manual review of flagged issues,' ensuring both speed and accuracy. This change impacts 'Cost Structure' (software acquisition) but reinforces the value proposition.

quiz.question: What is the primary purpose of a value proposition?
options: To list all the features of a product or service.
To explain why a customer should choose your offering over alternatives.
To detail the company's internal resources and capabilities.
To outline the company's financial projections and expected profits.
quiz.explanation: The primary purpose of a value proposition is to clearly articulate the unique benefits and reasons for a customer to choose a particular offering, differentiating it from competitors. Listing features (option 0) is part of it, but not the core purpose. Options 2 and 3 describe internal aspects or outcomes, not the customer-facing value.

quiz.question: Is owning a high-tech manufacturing plant enough to form a strong value proposition?
options: Yes, because a valuable resource is always a strong value proposition.
No, because a value proposition must explain the customer benefit derived from that resource.
Yes, if the plant is the only one of its kind in the market.
No, unless the plant produces a product that is entirely unique.
quiz.explanation: Owning a resource, no matter how advanced, is not a value proposition in itself. A value proposition must articulate the specific benefit or useful outcome that resource provides to the customer. The manufacturing plant is a means to an end, not the end value for the customer. Options 0 and 2 confuse resources with customer benefits. Option 3 is closer but still focuses on the product's uniqueness rather than the customer's gain.

quiz.question: A startup promises 'instant, personalized customer support' but plans to use only a single, part-time customer service agent. What is the most likely issue?
options: The startup will struggle to find enough customers.
The value proposition is too broad and lacks focus.
There is an inconsistency between the value proposition and key activities/resources.
The pricing model will be too high for the target market.
quiz.explanation: The promise of 'instant, personalized customer support' is a strong value proposition. However, relying on a 'single, part-time customer service agent' as a key resource and activity creates a clear inconsistency. This operational setup cannot realistically deliver instant or personalized support, leading to customer dissatisfaction. Options 0, 1, and 3 are possible business challenges but not the direct, most likely issue stemming from this specific conflict.

quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT a core component of a business model?
options: Key Activities
Customer Segments
Competitor Analysis
Revenue Streams
quiz.explanation: Key Activities, Customer Segments, and Revenue Streams are all fundamental components of a business model, describing how a company operates to create and capture value. Competitor Analysis is a crucial part of market research and strategy, but it is not typically considered a direct component *within* the business model canvas itself, which focuses on the internal workings and value exchange of the business.

quiz.question: A local bakery's value proposition is 'freshly baked, artisanal bread delivered to your door daily.' What is a critical assumption they should test?
options: That all customers eat bread daily.
That customers are willing to pay a premium for daily delivery of artisanal bread.
That the bakery can bake bread.
That there are no other bakeries in town.
quiz.explanation: The value proposition implies convenience (delivery) and quality (artisanal, freshly baked). A critical assumption is whether customers perceive enough value in this combination to justify the associated cost, which would likely be higher due to delivery and artisanal production. Option 0 is too broad and unlikely to be true for all. Option 2 is a basic operational capability, not an assumption about customer behavior. Option 3 is an external market factor, not a direct assumption tied to the value proposition's core offering.

quiz.question: When evaluating a business model, why is 'coherence' more important than simply 'filling all the boxes'?
options: Because a complete model with all boxes filled guarantees success.
Because coherence ensures all elements work together to deliver the value proposition sustainably.
Because filling boxes is a legal requirement for business registration.
Because coherence makes the model easier to present to investors.
quiz.explanation: Coherence means that all parts of the business model (customer segments, channels, activities, resources, revenue, costs) logically align and support the value proposition. This interconnectedness is vital for the business to function effectively and sustainably deliver its promised value. Simply filling boxes without this alignment can lead to a dysfunctional or unprofitable business. Options 0, 2, and 3 are incorrect; a complete model doesn't guarantee success, it's not a legal requirement, and while it might help with presentations, that's not its primary importance.

assignment.prompt: Develop a value proposition and a simplified business model for a new fictional service or product. Identify one potential inconsistency and propose a solution.
criteria: Value proposition is clear, concise, and customer-centric.
Business model elements are logically connected to the value proposition.
Each element includes a plausible assumption and a test.
One clear inconsistency between elements is identified.
A practical and coherent solution to the inconsistency is proposed.

rubric.excellent: Clearly articulates a unique customer benefit and reason to choose, in two concise sentences.
rubric.adequate: States a benefit but may lack uniqueness or be slightly vague, in two sentences.
rubric.needsRevision: Vague, focuses on features, or exceeds two sentences; unclear customer benefit.

rubric.excellent: All five business model elements are directly and logically linked to the value proposition, showing strong coherence.
rubric.adequate: Most business model elements are linked to the value proposition, but some connections might be weak or unclear.
rubric.needsRevision: Business model elements are listed but show little to no clear connection to the value proposition.

rubric.excellent: Each of the five business model elements includes a specific, plausible assumption and a practical, measurable test.
rubric.adequate: Assumptions and tests are present for most elements, but some may be generic or less practical.
rubric.needsRevision: Missing assumptions or tests for multiple elements, or those provided are irrelevant/untestable.

rubric.excellent: Identifies a clear, significant inconsistency between the value proposition and a business model element, or between two elements.
rubric.adequate: Identifies a minor inconsistency, or the identified issue is not a direct conflict within the model.
rubric.needsRevision: Fails to identify any inconsistency, or the identified issue is not a true conflict within the business model.

rubric.excellent: Proposes a practical, well-reasoned solution that directly addresses the identified inconsistency and improves model coherence.
rubric.adequate: Proposes a solution that addresses the inconsistency, but it may lack detail or full coherence.
rubric.needsRevision: No solution proposed, or the proposed solution does not effectively resolve the identified inconsistency.

faq.question: What's the difference between a value proposition and a mission statement?
faq.answer: A value proposition focuses on the specific benefits and reasons why a customer should choose your product or service. A mission statement, on the other hand, describes the overall purpose and goals of the organization, often broader and more internally focused.

faq.question: Can a business have multiple value propositions?
faq.answer: Yes, a business can have different value propositions for different customer segments. For example, a software company might have one value proposition for individual users and another for corporate clients, each addressing distinct needs and offering unique benefits.

faq.question: How often should I review my value proposition and business model?
faq.answer: You should review your value proposition and business model regularly, especially when there are significant changes in the market, technology, customer needs, or your own business capabilities. It's an iterative process, not a one-time task, to ensure continued relevance and competitiveness.

summary: A value proposition clearly defines the customer, their problem, the useful outcome, and why your offering is superior.
A business model connects the value proposition to key elements like customers, channels, activities, resources, revenue, and costs.
Coherence between all business model elements is crucial for sustainable value delivery.
Regularly identify and resolve inconsistencies to ensure your business model effectively supports your value proposition.

title: Channels, selling and customer experience
intro: Every business needs a way to reach its customers and deliver its products or services. This path, known as a channel, is crucial for sales and overall customer satisfaction. Understanding how customers interact with your business at each stage of their journey, from first hearing about you to making a purchase and beyond, helps you identify opportunities for improvement. This lesson will explore the concept of channels, how they relate to the customer journey, and how to measure their effectiveness to enhance the customer experience.
goals: Define what a channel is and its role in the customer journey.
Identify the key stages of a customer journey and the elements within each stage.
Calculate conversion rates at different points in the customer journey.
Propose improvements to a customer journey based on identified friction points.

sections.title: Understanding Channels and Customer Journeys
sections.text: A channel is simply the path an offer takes to reach a customer. This can be a physical store, a website, a social media platform, or even a phone call. It's important to note that the channel used to present an offer might be different from the channel used for delivery or customer support. For example, a customer might discover a product on social media (awareness channel), order it online (selling channel), and receive support via email (support channel). The customer journey maps the entire sequence of interactions a customer has with a company, from initial awareness to post-purchase activities. It typically includes stages like Awareness, Enquiry, Order, Receipt, and Return. Each stage presents unique questions for the customer, requires specific information from the business, and can introduce friction points that might deter a customer from proceeding.
sections.reflection: Think about a recent purchase you made. What channels did you use to discover the product, make the purchase, and receive it? Were these channels different?

sections.title: Mapping the Customer Journey Process
sections.text: To effectively manage channels and customer experience, you need to map out the customer journey. This involves identifying each stage a customer goes through. For each stage, consider: What question does the customer have? What information do they need from us? What potential obstacles or 'friction' might they encounter? Who within our organization is responsible for this stage? And how do we measure success or failure at this point? For instance, in the 'Awareness' stage, a customer might ask, 'What problem does this product solve?' They need clear marketing messages. Friction could be confusing advertisements. The marketing team is responsible, and 'website visits' or 'social media impressions' might be key measures. By systematically detailing these elements for every stage, businesses can pinpoint weaknesses and areas for improvement.
sections.reflection: Choose a simple service, like ordering food online. Try to map out its customer journey, identifying a customer question, information needed, and potential friction for each stage.

sections.title: Using Channel Insights for Improvement
sections.text: Understanding your channels and customer journey isn't just an academic exercise; it's a powerful tool for business improvement. By analyzing the journey, you can identify 'leakage points' where customers drop off. For example, if many customers add items to their cart but don't complete the purchase, there's a significant leakage point in the 'Order' stage. Insights gained from this analysis can inform strategic decisions. Perhaps the checkout process is too complicated, or shipping costs are unexpectedly high. Addressing these specific friction points can lead to higher conversion rates, increased sales, and a more positive customer experience. This proactive approach ensures that resources are directed towards the most impactful changes, leading to tangible business benefits and stronger customer relationships.
sections.reflection: Consider a time you abandoned a purchase online. What was the specific friction point that made you stop? How could the business have improved that experience?

sections.title: Limitations of Channel Analysis
sections.text: While channel analysis is valuable, it has limitations. One common pitfall is comparing channels without a consistent definition of cost and measurement window. For example, comparing the 'cost per acquisition' of a social media campaign run for a week to an email campaign run for a month will yield misleading results. The measurement window must be consistent to ensure a fair comparison. Similarly, the definition of 'cost' must be comprehensive, including not just advertising spend but also staff time, technology, and overhead. Another limitation is that channel performance can fluctuate due to external factors like seasonality, competitor actions, or economic changes, which might not be immediately apparent in the data. Always consider the broader context when interpreting channel performance metrics to avoid drawing incorrect conclusions.
sections.reflection: Why might comparing 'website visitors' from an online ad campaign to 'foot traffic' from a print ad campaign be problematic? What factors would you need to consider for a fair comparison?

sections.title: Avoiding Common Errors in Measurement
sections.text: A frequent mistake in channel analysis is equating 'views' or 'impressions' with 'sales.' While views indicate awareness, they do not directly translate to revenue. A high number of views with low sales suggests a problem with conversion, not necessarily with awareness. Another critical error involves misinterpreting conversion rates due to different denominators. For instance, a 'visit-to-order' conversion rate will naturally be lower than an 'enquiry-to-order' conversion rate because the starting pool of 'enquiries' is already more qualified than 'visits.' Using the wrong denominator changes the meaning of the percentage, not the underlying performance of the service. Always be clear about what transition your conversion rate is measuring to ensure accurate interpretation and avoid drawing faulty conclusions about channel effectiveness.
sections.reflection: If a website has 1000 visitors and 10 sales, and 100 enquiries and 10 sales, how would you describe the difference in performance between 'visitors' and 'enquiries' as starting points?

sections.title: Transferring Channel Insights to New Contexts
sections.text: The principles of channel analysis and customer journey mapping are highly transferable across various industries and business models. Whether you're selling physical products, offering digital services, or running a non-profit, understanding how your audience discovers, engages with, and ultimately uses your offering is paramount. For a B2B company, the 'awareness' stage might involve industry conferences, while for a local cafe, it could be street signage. The 'order' stage for a software company might be a free trial sign-up, whereas for a consultant, it's a signed contract. The core methodology—identifying stages, customer questions, friction, owners, and measures—remains consistent. By applying this structured approach, you can optimize any customer interaction flow, leading to improved efficiency, higher satisfaction, and better outcomes regardless of the specific context.
sections.reflection: How might the customer journey for a public library differ from that of an online clothing store? What stages might be similar, and which would be unique?

example.title: Analyzing Customer Conversion Rates
example.text: This is a fictional learning case. A new online service aimed at helping small businesses manage their finances wants to understand how effective its channels are. Over a specific period, their website recorded 100 visits. From these visits, 20 customers submitted an enquiry form to learn more about the service. Out of those 20 enquiries, 5 customers ultimately signed up for a paid subscription. The team wants to understand the conversion rates at different stages.
example.decision: To accurately assess channel effectiveness, it's crucial to calculate conversion rates at each relevant stage of the customer journey, using the correct denominator for each calculation. This helps pinpoint where customers are progressing and where they might be dropping off.
steps: Step 1: Calculate Visit-to-Enquiry Conversion. This measures how many website visitors become interested enough to make an enquiry. We divide the number of enquiries by the total number of visits: 20 enquiries / 100 visits = 0.20. Multiplied by 100, this gives us a 20% conversion rate. This shows that one-fifth of visitors take the next step.

Step 2: Calculate Visit-to-Order Conversion. This measures the overall effectiveness of the channel from initial awareness to final purchase. We divide the number of orders by the total number of visits: 5 orders / 100 visits = 0.05. Multiplied by 100, this results in a 5% conversion rate. This is a broad measure of the entire funnel.

Step 3: Calculate Enquiry-to-Order Conversion. This measures how effective the sales process is after a customer has shown initial interest. We divide the number of orders by the number of enquiries: 5 orders / 20 enquiries = 0.25. Multiplied by 100, this gives us a 25% conversion rate. This specific rate indicates the strength of the follow-up and sales pitch.

Step 4: Understand the Impact of Denominators. Notice that the visit-to-order conversion (5%) is different from the enquiry-to-order conversion (25%). This isn't because the service's performance changed, but because the starting point (denominator) for the calculation is different. The 5% reflects the entire journey from a broad audience, while the 25% reflects conversion from a more qualified, interested group.

Step 5: Identify Potential Leakage Points. The significant drop from 100 visits to 20 enquiries (80% leakage) suggests that the initial website content or call to action might need improvement to capture more interest. The drop from 20 enquiries to 5 orders (75% leakage) indicates that the sales follow-up or product offering for interested customers could also be refined.

quiz.question: What is the primary purpose of mapping a customer journey?
options: To identify all employees involved in customer service.
To understand the sequence of customer interactions and identify improvement areas.
To track competitor activities and market trends.
To calculate the total revenue generated by each customer.
quiz.explanation: Mapping a customer journey helps businesses visualize the entire path a customer takes, from initial contact to post-purchase. This process is crucial for identifying pain points, friction, and opportunities to enhance the customer experience and improve conversion rates, not just for internal staffing or competitor analysis.

quiz.question: A company has 500 website visitors, 100 sign-ups for a free trial, and 20 paid subscriptions. What is the conversion rate from free trial sign-up to paid subscription?
quiz.explanation: To calculate the conversion rate from free trial sign-up to paid subscription, you divide the number of paid subscriptions by the number of free trial sign-ups: 20 paid subscriptions / 100 free trial sign-ups = 0.20. Multiplied by 100, this is 20%. The other options represent different calculations or incorrect arithmetic.

quiz.question: Which of the following best describes 'friction' in a customer journey?
options: A positive interaction that encourages a customer to proceed.
Any obstacle or difficulty that might prevent a customer from moving to the next stage.
The total cost a customer pays for a product or service.
The speed at which a customer completes a transaction.
quiz.explanation: Friction refers to any point in the customer journey where a customer encounters difficulty, confusion, or resistance, potentially causing them to abandon the process. It's an obstacle, not a positive interaction, cost, or speed measurement.

quiz.question: A marketing team reports 10,000 views on a new advertisement and 50 sales. The sales team reports 500 enquiries from the ad, leading to the same 50 sales. Which statement is most accurate?
options: The ad is highly effective because it generated 10,000 views.
The sales team is underperforming because only 50 sales resulted from 500 enquiries.
Views are not sales: view-to-sale conversion is 0.5%, while enquiry-to-sale conversion is 10%.
The ad cost too much given the low number of sales.
quiz.explanation: The two rates use different denominators: 50 divided by 10,000 is 0.5%, and 50 divided by 500 is 10%. Both can describe the same 50 sales at different journey stages. Neither rate alone establishes whether the campaign or sales team performed well; that requires costs, comparable definitions and an appropriate benchmark.

quiz.question: Why is it problematic to compare the performance of a social media channel measured over one week with an email marketing channel measured over one month?
options: Social media campaigns are always more effective than email campaigns.
The different measurement windows make the comparison inconsistent and potentially misleading.
Customers prefer social media over email for product discovery.
Email marketing is generally more expensive than social media marketing.
quiz.explanation: Comparing channels requires consistent measurement parameters, including the time window. A one-week social media campaign cannot be fairly compared to a one-month email campaign because the longer duration for email allows for more interactions and conversions, skewing the results. The other options are assumptions or generalizations not directly related to the measurement inconsistency.

quiz.question: In the example provided in the lesson, what was the enquiry-to-order conversion rate?
quiz.explanation: The example stated 20 enquiries and 5 orders. The enquiry-to-order conversion is calculated by dividing the number of orders by the number of enquiries: 5 orders / 20 enquiries = 0.25, or 25%. This measures how effectively enquiries are converted into actual purchases.

assignment.prompt: Imagine you are launching a new online course. Map out a five-stage customer journey for this course, from initial awareness to post-course engagement. For each stage, identify the customer's question, potential friction points, the team or person responsible, and a key metric to measure success. Then, identify one stage with the highest 'leakage' (where most customers drop off), propose a specific change to reduce this leakage, and explain how you would measure the impact of this change without altering the definition of your conversion rate.
criteria: Clear identification of five distinct customer journey stages.
For each stage, a relevant customer question, friction point, responsible party, and measurable metric are provided.
A plausible 'leakage' point is identified within one of the stages.
A specific, actionable change is proposed to address the identified leakage.
A clear, consistent method for measuring the impact of the proposed change is described, maintaining the original conversion rate definition.

rubric.excellent: Clearly defines five distinct and logical stages for the online course customer journey.
rubric.adequate: Defines five stages, but some may overlap or lack distinctiveness.
rubric.needsRevision: Fewer than five stages, or stages are unclear/illogical.

rubric.excellent: Provides highly relevant and specific details for customer question, friction, responsible party, and metric for ALL five stages.
rubric.adequate: Provides details for most stages, but some elements may be generic or less relevant.
rubric.needsRevision: Missing elements for multiple stages, or details are vague/irrelevant.

rubric.excellent: Identifies a highly plausible and impactful leakage point within one of the stages, with clear reasoning.
rubric.adequate: Identifies a leakage point, but its impact or reasoning could be stronger.
rubric.needsRevision: Fails to identify a specific leakage point or provides an unconvincing one.

rubric.excellent: Proposes a highly specific, creative, and actionable change directly addressing the identified leakage point.
rubric.adequate: Proposes a change that addresses the leakage, but it may be somewhat generic or less impactful.
rubric.needsRevision: Proposes a vague change, or one that does not directly address the leakage point.

rubric.excellent: Clearly and precisely describes how the impact of the change will be measured, ensuring the conversion rate definition remains consistent.
rubric.adequate: Describes a method for measurement, but it may lack some precision or clarity regarding consistency.
rubric.needsRevision: Fails to describe a measurement method, or the method alters the original conversion rate definition.

faq.question: What's the difference between a channel and a touchpoint?
faq.answer: A channel is the broad path or medium through which a customer interacts with your business (e.g., website, social media, physical store). A touchpoint is a specific interaction within that channel or across channels (e.g., clicking an ad, reading a product description, speaking to a sales representative). A channel contains many touchpoints.

faq.question: Why is it important to identify 'friction' in the customer journey?
faq.answer: Identifying friction points is crucial because they are moments where customers might get frustrated, confused, or encounter obstacles, leading them to abandon their journey. By pinpointing and resolving these friction points, businesses can improve customer satisfaction, increase conversion rates, and enhance overall efficiency.

faq.question: Can a single channel serve multiple stages of the customer journey?
faq.answer: Yes, absolutely. For example, a company's website can serve as an awareness channel (through blog posts), an enquiry channel (through contact forms), an order channel (e-commerce checkout), and even a support channel (FAQ section or live chat). The key is to optimize each function within that channel for its specific stage.

summary: A channel is the path an offer takes to reach a customer, distinct from delivery or support.
The customer journey maps interactions through stages like Awareness, Enquiry, Order, Receipt, and Return, each with questions, information, and friction.
Conversion rates measure progress between stages, but views are not sales, and denominators must be consistent for accurate comparison.
Mapping the journey helps identify leakage points and inform targeted improvements to enhance customer experience and sales.

Scene 2: Focus on a specific stage (e.g., 'Order'). Show a customer encountering a 'friction point' (e.g., a complex online form or unexpected shipping fees) represented by a red 'X' or a roadblock. title: Pricing, contribution and break-even
intro: A price change affects the amount left from every sale, not just the number of customers who buy. In this lesson you will build a small contribution model, test a proposed discount and explain what the model cannot establish. All amounts and businesses in the worked case are fictional; use a single currency and one month throughout.
goals: Calculate contribution per order from price and variable cost.
Calculate whole-order break-even volume with positive contribution.
Compare a discount using both break-even and a target contribution.
State the assumptions and capacity checks needed before a pricing decision.

sections.title: What one sale contributes
sections.text: Revenue is the amount earned from sales before the costs in this model are deducted. A variable cost changes with the number of orders: packaging used for each order is one possible example. A fixed cost stays unchanged within a stated activity range and period, such as an agreed monthly equipment rental. Contribution per order is price minus variable cost per order. It is the amount available to cover fixed costs and then contribute to an operating result. It is not automatically profit, and receiving cash is a separate question. In our fictional case, an order priced at 150 with variable cost of 90 contributes 60. Describe the order consistently: changing its size or included service changes the meaning of the calculation.
sections.reflection: Which costs in a service you know would increase with each additional order, and which would stay unchanged for one month?

sections.title: Finding break-even carefully
sections.text: Break-even volume is the number of orders at which total contribution equals the fixed costs included in the model. With contribution of 60 per order and monthly fixed costs of 900, divide 900 by 60 to obtain 15 orders per month. At that volume, revenue is 2,250 and variable costs are 1,350, leaving exactly 900 to cover the fixed costs. When orders cannot be divided, round a non-integer result upward. A result of 15.2 requires 16 whole orders to avoid a loss under the assumptions. Do not apply this division mechanically when contribution is zero or negative: additional sales would not cover positive fixed costs. Always state the period and check that the expected volume remains within the assumed capacity range.
sections.reflection: Why does rounding a break-even volume of 15.2 down to 15 give an unsafe conclusion?

sections.title: Evaluating a proposed discount
sections.text: A lower price can increase demand, but this response is an assumption to test, not a consequence of the formula. Reduce the fictional price from 150 to 140 while holding variable cost at 90. Contribution falls from 60 to 50, so break-even rises from 15 to 18 monthly orders. This comparison answers how many orders cover the included fixed costs; it does not answer how many preserve the previous result. If the original plan sold 20 orders, it generated total contribution of 1,200. To preserve that contribution at 50 per order requires 24 orders, or four more than before. A discount can therefore reach break-even while still producing a worse result than the original plan. Name the target before selecting a volume.
sections.reflection: What is the difference between reaching 18 orders and reaching 24 orders in this discount proposal?

sections.title: Recognising the model limits
sections.text: This simple model assumes one consistent order type, constant price and variable cost per order, and fixed costs that remain constant over the relevant volume range. A capacity threshold can invalidate those assumptions. For example, fulfilling extra orders might require a second rental contract, overtime or a different supplier price. Rebuild the model when those conditions change instead of extrapolating the old result. The result also excludes any costs not explicitly listed, as well as taxes and financing effects. It is a simplified operating result, not a claim about net profit. Timing matters separately: a profitable order can require cash for materials before the customer pays. A decision should therefore consider capacity and cash timing alongside contribution.
sections.reflection: Which assumption would you revisit first if the discounted volume required a second worker or another machine?

sections.title: Avoiding misleading comparisons
sections.text: Keep units and time periods consistent. A monthly fixed cost cannot be compared directly with daily contribution unless you explicitly convert the activity into the same month using a stated number of operating days. Do not confuse contribution per order with contribution margin as a percentage of revenue. In the original case the amount is 60, while the percentage is 60 divided by 150, or 40 percent. After the discount the amount is 50 and the percentage is about 35.7 percent. Neither number establishes demand. Another error is to subtract fixed costs twice: once through an allocated amount inside the variable cost and again as a monthly total. Explain your cost classification so another person can reproduce it and identify omissions.
sections.reflection: How would you detect that a monthly rental had been counted inside unit cost and then deducted again?

sections.title: Turning the calculation into a decision
sections.text: Use the model to compare explicit alternatives and plan a limited test. Record the current price, proposed price, estimated variable cost, included fixed costs and available capacity for the same period. Calculate the volume required for each objective, then compare that volume with evidence about demand. In the fictional case, a small discount trial should measure completed paid orders, cancellations, actual variable cost and the time needed to serve each order. Set a review date and a maximum commitment before starting. If 24 discounted orders cannot be delivered without extra costs, revise the scenario before accepting it. A sound recommendation can be to keep the current price, test a narrower offer or gather more evidence; calculating a positive result alone does not justify expansion.
sections.reflection: What would you measure during a discount trial to distinguish increased interest from sustainable additional sales?

example.title: A fictional monthly pricing decision
example.text: This is a fictional learning case. A small service plans to sell 20 identical orders this month at 150 each. Variable cost is 90 per order and the fixed costs included in the model total 900 for the month. The owner is considering a price of 140. Assume one currency, no additional fixed costs within the tested range and unchanged variable cost; demand and available capacity still need checking.
example.decision: Compare covering fixed costs with preserving the original operating result, then identify what evidence would justify a discount.
steps: At the current price, contribution per order is 150 − 90 = 60. For 20 orders, revenue is 3,000 and variable costs are 1,800, giving total contribution of 1,200. Deducting the included monthly fixed costs of 900 leaves a simplified operating result of 300, before excluded costs and taxes.

Current break-even is 900 ÷ 60 = 15 whole orders per month. At 15 orders, total contribution is 900 and exactly covers the included fixed costs. This is a threshold under the stated assumptions, not a forecast of customer demand or a guarantee that cash will be available when needed.

At the proposed price, contribution is 140 − 90 = 50 per order. The new break-even volume is 900 ÷ 50 = 18 orders per month. At an unchanged volume of 20, the simplified operating result becomes 20 × 50 − 900 = 100, which is 200 below the original result.

To preserve the original result of 300, required contribution is 900 + 300 = 1,200. Divide by the new contribution of 50 to obtain 24 orders. That is four more orders than the original 20, a 20 percent increase in volume. The formula specifies the required increase but does not show that customers will provide it.

Before choosing the discount, check whether 24 orders can be delivered within the same cost and capacity assumptions, and whether a small test supports sufficient paid demand. If additional staffing or equipment changes costs, calculate a new scenario. Record payment timing separately and select a review date rather than treating the model as a final forecast.

quiz.question: An order sells for 150 and has variable cost of 90. What is contribution per order?
quiz.explanation: Contribution is price minus variable cost: 150 minus 90 equals 60. Revenue and variable cost alone do not measure the amount available to cover fixed costs.

quiz.question: Monthly fixed costs are 900 and contribution is 50 per order. What volume covers these costs?
options: 15 orders
18 orders
20 orders
24 orders
quiz.explanation: Dividing 900 by 50 gives 18 whole orders per month. Twenty-four answers a different question: preserving the original contribution of 1,200.

quiz.question: The original 20 orders contributed 60 each. After a discount each contributes 50. How many orders preserve total contribution?
quiz.explanation: The original contribution is 20 times 60, or 1,200. Dividing by 50 gives 24 orders; merely reaching break-even would not preserve the previous result.

quiz.question: A model produces break-even volume of 15.2 indivisible orders. Which minimum volume avoids a loss under its assumptions?
quiz.explanation: Round up to 16 whole orders because 15 provide less than the contribution required. Fractional orders are unavailable in this scenario, so ordinary rounding is inappropriate.

quiz.question: The discount would require a second monthly equipment rental. What should happen next?
options: Keep the old fixed cost because price is lower
Recalculate with the extra rental and check capacity
Ignore fixed costs once contribution is positive
Assume extra sales always pay for the rental
quiz.explanation: The extra rental changes the fixed-cost assumption and therefore the required volume. Positive contribution alone does not prove that the additional monthly commitment can be covered.

quiz.question: Price and variable cost are both 90, with positive monthly fixed costs. What does the simple model imply?
options: Every sale covers some fixed cost
Nine orders always break even
No finite sales volume covers those fixed costs at zero contribution
Break-even is fixed cost divided by 90
quiz.explanation: Contribution is zero, so no amount remains from each order to cover positive fixed costs. Dividing by revenue would incorrectly ignore the equally large variable cost.

assignment.prompt: Build a one-month pricing decision sheet for the fictional service. Compare the current and proposed prices, calculate two different volume targets, and revise one cost assumption before recommending a limited test.
fields: Scope: currency, month, order definition and included costs
Calculation table: contribution and break-even for both prices
Target comparison: volume preserving the original result
Revised scenario: one changed cost or capacity assumption
Decision note: demand evidence, cash timing and test review date
criteria: Units and period are explicit and consistent.
Both contribution and break-even calculations can be reproduced.
Break-even and preservation of the original result are distinguished.
The revised assumption is reflected throughout the calculations.
The recommendation states evidence needed and a bounded next step.

rubric.excellent: Defines all units, the monthly period, order type and exclusions without mixing fixed and variable costs.
rubric.adequate: Defines the monthly period and order type but leaves one exclusion unclear.
rubric.needsRevision: Mixes periods or leaves the cost classification undefined.

rubric.excellent: Shows 60 and 50 contribution, 15 and 18 break-even orders, with formulas and whole-order rounding where needed.
rubric.adequate: Obtains the main values but omits one formula or rounding explanation.
rubric.needsRevision: Uses revenue instead of contribution or calculates an incorrect threshold.

rubric.excellent: Explains why 24 orders preserve 1,200 contribution and why 18 only covers fixed costs.
rubric.adequate: Calculates 24 orders but gives a limited explanation of the two targets.
rubric.needsRevision: Treats reaching break-even as equivalent to preserving the original result.

rubric.excellent: States a changed assumption and consistently recomputes its affected values and limitations.
rubric.adequate: States and calculates a plausible change but misses one affected comparison.
rubric.needsRevision: Changes a cost in prose while retaining incompatible original results.

rubric.excellent: Links a bounded trial to paid demand, capacity, cash timing and a stated review date.
rubric.adequate: Suggests a limited trial with a measurement but leaves one operational check unspecified.
rubric.needsRevision: Claims the formula guarantees sales or recommends an unlimited commitment without evidence.

faq.question: Does a positive contribution mean the business is profitable?
faq.answer: No. Total contribution must first cover the fixed costs included in the period. Other omitted costs, taxes and financing can also change the final result.

faq.question: Can I use the same formula for several different products?
faq.answer: Only after modelling the mix carefully. Products may have different contributions, so an average depends on an explicit sales mix that can change. This lesson holds one order type constant.

faq.question: Does reaching break-even solve a cash shortage?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. Customers may pay after materials and wages are due. Prepare a separate schedule of cash inflows and outflows before making commitments.

summary: Contribution per order equals price minus variable cost per order.
With positive contribution, divide period fixed costs by unit contribution and round up for whole orders.
A discount can increase the sales volume needed both to break even and to preserve an earlier result.
Demand, relevant capacity, excluded costs and cash timing require separate checks.

readingVisuals.caption: Fictional amounts in one currency; fixed costs stay unchanged within the tested activity range.

readingVisuals.caption: Contribution and the operating result are different steps; neither is a cash balance.

Scene 2: A calendar and workshop fill with customer appointments after a proposed discount. Contrast the ease of announcing a lower price with the extra work needed to complete four more orders; do not reproduce the reading flow or numeric table.
